events.ai_basis: In the preparation of this work, AI models were used to suggest initial exploratory directions, assist with computations, and proofread earlier versions of the manuscript. The author independently reconstructed and verified all the mathematical content that came from the models, and assumes full responsibility for the paper.
The models suggested an argument leading to a bound of the form (N(log log N)^2 on h(E)); the author verified and reconstructed that argument.

why: The statement is the weak epsilon-form: a lower bound c(eps) x^(1/2-eps) on |y^2-x^3|. Danilov's family and Elkies's 46.60 record bear only on the exponent-1/2 form with a fixed constant (Hall's original form), not on the epsilon-form, so they are variants; the searches to finite ranges are instances; polynomial analogues and the gap-spacing result are variants; Browning-Chan and Badziahin use Hall-type hypotheses and prove nothing about it (none). Stark's 1973 log-scale separation and Pasten's 2026 Theorem 1.2 both lower-bound the very gap |x^3-y^2| unconditionally, so they are bounds on the quantity the conjecture is about, however far from a power of x; the problem stays open, direction null. Close call on Pasten's AI role: the disclosure is generic, but it explicitly says there was 'mathematical content that came from the models' which the author reconstructed and kept, beyond proofreading and computation; I read that as part of the mathematics in the paper and answered assisted, though it does not say which theorem. The Szpiro paper's quote credits a model-suggested argument (assisted) but the event does not bear on Hall (none), so it is discarded regardless.
doubts: Pasten's AI disclosure does not attribute any content to Theorem 1.2 specifically, and the quote came through a summarising fetch tool; a reading of 'none' (exploratory suggestions only) is defensible. Whether a (log X)^2 separation counts as a bound on this problem rather than a different quantity is also arguable; I counted it because it lower-bounds the same gap for all integers. Stark 1973's separation bound is inferred from Pasten's comparison ('improving Stark's (log X)^(1-o(1))'), not from Stark's paper.
